title: Born blind in poverty, he captained India to two cricket World Cups. October 15, 2026.
excerpt: From the scientist-president born this day in 1931, to a cybersecurity CEO honored as a great American immigrant, to a couple who gave their old engineering college a record gift - October 15's five stories are about turning a starting disadvantage into the foundation for something larger.
bodyHtml:
Today's five stories share a quiet thread: each one starts from a position that looks like a disadvantage - a fisherman's village, a foreign country with no safety net, a childhood of poverty and blindness, a transit system with no prior ridership habit to build on - and ends somewhere far past where that starting point would predict.

October 15, 1931: a fisherman's son was born in Rameswaram. He would go on to run India's missile program and its presidency

Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam joined DRDO in 1958 and ISRO in 1969, led development of missiles like Agni and Prithvi, played a central role in the 1998 Pokhran-II tests, and served as India's 11th President from 2002 to 2007.

He went from an IIT engineering degree to running one of the world's biggest cybersecurity companies. Carnegie just named him one of America's great immigrants

Nikesh Arora, born in Ghaziabad and chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks since 2018, was named to Carnegie Corporation's 2026 Great Immigrants, Great Americans list - one of four Indian Americans honored this year.

A US couple just gave their old engineering college a record $4 million

Chand P. Garg, a 1968 BITS Pilani mechanical engineering graduate now based in the US, and his wife Manju Garg pledged $4 million to the institute's endowment - the largest individual gift it has ever received, funding scholarships for about 16 students a year.

Mumbai Metro just crossed 300 million passenger journeys

Mumbai's metro network hit 300 million cumulative passenger journeys on August 3, 2026, with the last 50 million arriving in just 179 days - the fastest growth in the network's history, driven partly by new lines opened in April 2026.

Born blind in poverty, he captained India to two cricket World Cups

Shekhar Naik, born blind to a poor family in Shimoga, Karnataka, captained India's blind cricket team to World Cup titles in 2012 and 2014, scoring 134 off 58 balls in the 2012 final, and became the first blind cricketer to receive the Padma Shri.

Five stories, one pattern: a fisherman's son who became a scientist-president, an engineering graduate who ended up running global cybersecurity, a six-decade-old debt of gratitude repaid in record size, a transit system whose growth keeps accelerating rather than slowing, and a blind captain who read the game well enough to win it twice.
